nameStory: The snowshoe hare gets its name from its impressively oversized hind feet that work just like snowshoes! These big, furry paws spread the hare's weight across snow, preventing it from sinking in during winter hops. It's also called the 'varying hare' because its fur dramatically changes color with the seasons.
description: The snowshoe hare is a medium-sized rabbit relative about the size of a small house cat, weighing 2-4 pounds. Its most striking feature is its seasonal color change - rusty brown fur in summer that transforms to bright white in winter, with year-round white flanks. Unlike typical rabbits, it has relatively short ears tipped with distinctive black tufts and those famous oversized hind feet. This nocturnal hopper doesn't hibernate and stays active all winter long.

idTips.label: Seasonal Fur
idTips.description: Coat changes from rusty brown in summer to brilliant white in winter, with flanks staying white year-round. The winter coat feels incredibly dense and soft, almost like touching a plush toy.

idTips.label: Feet
idTips.description: Hind feet are noticeably oversized compared to body size, densely furred on the bottom like built-in slippers. Tracks show distinctly large rear paw prints in snow.

idTips.label: Ears
idTips.description: Ears are shorter than most rabbits and hares, with distinctive black fur tufts along the edges that remain dark even in winter coat.

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Most active at dawn and dusk, often seen in small feeding groups. Moves in characteristic bounding hops rather than running smoothly.

idTips.label: Sign
idTips.description: Look for gnawed bark on trees and shrubs in winter, especially aspen and birch. Pellets are round and fibrous, often found in small clusters near feeding areas.

habitat: Snowshoe hares prefer dense coniferous and mixed forests with thick understory for cover, especially areas with young growth and forest edges. They thrive in northern New England's spruce-fir forests, particularly where logging or natural disturbances have created brushy regeneration. You'll find them from sea level up into mountain forests, wherever there's adequate winter snow cover.

seasonality.spring: Brown summer coat begins growing in, creating a patchy brown-and-white appearance. Young are born in shallow depressions lined with fur.
seasonality.summer: Full rusty-brown coat with white flanks clearly visible. Most active feeding period on grasses, ferns, and leafy plants in forest clearings.
seasonality.fall: White winter coat grows in patches, creating mottled appearance. Begins switching to woody diet of twigs and bark.
seasonality.winter: Brilliant white coat provides snow camouflage. Most easily spotted against dark tree trunks, feeding on bark and twigs in early morning or evening.

funFact: Snowshoe hares and Canada lynx populations rise and fall together in a famous 10-year cycle - when hare numbers crash, lynx numbers follow two years later, then when lynx become scarce, hare populations explode again, creating one of nature's most predictable population roller coasters!
confusionNotes: Often confused with cottontail rabbits, but snowshoe hares are larger with much bigger feet and shorter ears with black tips. Memory trick: if the ears look too short for a rabbit and the feet look too big, it's probably a snowshoe hare!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called the 'snowshoe rabbit,' this animal is actually a true hare - babies are born fully furred with eyes open, unlike rabbit babies which are born blind and hairless in burrows.
compareHints: The snowshoe hare is the only member of the true hare genus (Lepus) found in New England. Compared to cottontail rabbits in the same family, snowshoe hares are larger, change color seasonally, have shorter ears, and much larger hind feet. Their young are also born ready to hop, while cottontail babies are helpless at birth.
